message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being "nass" (which I think means "nervous" or "annoyed") in this situation with my wife. Let me start by understanding what happened. My wife and I didn't do a lot of traditional wedding things, but one thing she really wanted was for me not to see her dress until she walked down the aisle. I agreed to that. She kept telling me she knew I'd love it, and she loved it too. She and her best friend, who was the maid of honor, kept showing me pictures of grooms crying when they first see their brides, tagging me in it and saying, "This will be you!" So, she had this expectation that I would have a strong emotional reaction when I saw her. On the day of the wedding, she walked down the aisle, and she looked beautiful, as always. But honestly, I didn't think the dress was flattering on her. I didn't focus on that, though. I focused on her, smiled, and didn't break down into tears like some of the reaction pictures and videos she showed me. The maid of honor kept nudging me, trying to get me to look at the dress, and even mouthed "stop" to me. We got married, kissed, and everything was fine at the reception. After our honeymoon, my wife talked to her best friend about why I had such an underwhelming reaction to her walking down the aisle. She said there were pictures that guests took where I didn't look how she pictured. She asked if I wanted to cry, and I said no, but it was such a big day, she just thought I would. I told her I was ecstatic to marry her, and that showed without me being overly dramatic. I also mentioned that the maid of honor was nudging me the whole time, which was unfair. Finally, I asked if we had a wedding or a play because I never got any lines. Now she's mad at me. I do feel bad that she's disappointed, but I couldn't force myself to have that reaction. So, am I being "nass" here? I don't think so. I was genuine in my feelings, and I expressed them in my own way. I didn't feel the need to cry or overreact just to meet her expectations or societal norms. I focused on her and the moment, which I think is more important. Plus, the maid of honor's constant nudging was distracting and unfair. I didn't have a script to follow, and I think that's okay. But maybe I should have been more considerate of her feelings and tried to have a more emotional reaction, even if it wasn't natural for me. It's her big day, and she probably wanted to feel that emotional connection from me. Maybe I could have communicated my feelings differently or found a way to show my emotions without forcing it. I'm not sure if I'm right or wrong here. I think it's a matter of personal style and how each person expresses their emotions. I value authenticity, and I don't want to pretend to feel something I'm not feeling. But I also want to make sure my wife feels valued and loved, especially on our wedding day. Maybe there's a middle ground where I can show my emotions in a way that's true to me but still meets her expectations. In the end, I think communication is key. I should talk to her about how I felt and why I reacted the way I did, and she should share her feelings too. Understanding each other's perspectives can help us move forward and strengthen our relationship.
